O Thou of Little Faith
OH thow uv LIT-ul FAYTH
n. phr. (Christ's rebuke to Peter sinking on the water, after he had walked on it)
Greek oligopiste — a single compound vocative from oligos, little or few, and pistis, faith; the word is almost Christ's own, appearing in the New Testament only in His mouth.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Peter asked to come on the water, walked on it, saw the wind, was afraid, began to sink, and cried, Lord, save me. “And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?” The order of the sentence is the heart of it. The hand comes first and the rebuke after; the catching is not withheld until the faith improves. And the rebuke itself is precisely measured — little faith, not no faith, for the man had just walked on the sea at a word and his cry for rescue was itself an act of faith, rightly addressed. The word Christ uses here is one He uses of the anxious in the Sermon on the Mount and of the disciples in the storm and over the bread, always of true disciples whose faith is real and small. Scripture therefore gives us in this phrase a careful doctrine of weak faith: it is faith, it saves, it is rebuked, and it is held up by a hand stronger than itself. The Reformed divines made much of this against both presumption and despair, for a bruised reed is not broken, and he who prayed Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief was not sent away.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Little, small in quantity or degree; of small dignity or importance. Faith, the assent of the mind to the truth of what God has revealed; evangelical faith is the trust which the sinner reposes in Christ. O thou of little faith, Matthew 14:31, Christ's rebuke to a true but weak believer.

expand to see more

Little, small in quantity, extent, or degree; not much.

Faith, the assent of the mind to what God reveals, with trust in Christ.

Greek oligopistos, of little faith, a compound used in the New Testament by Christ alone.

Greek distazō, to waver, hesitate, or be of two minds — ‘wherefore didst thou doubt?’

Spoken while holding Peter, after he had walked on the sea, Matthew 14:29-31.

Key Scripture

Mat 14:31 — "And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?"

Mat 14:30 — "But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me."

Mat 8:26 — "And he saith unto them, Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith? Then he arose, and rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm."

Mar 9:24 — "And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief."

Modern Corruption

The phrase is pressed into a doctrine of faith as a force whose quantity secures outcomes, so that failure is always the believer's fault and weak faith is treated as no faith at all.

expand to see more

The word-of-faith teaching makes faith a measurable power and this verse its proof text: Peter sank because he did not have enough, and the sick or poor believer is told the same of his own case. The passage will not carry it. What saved Peter was not a quantity of faith but the hand of Christ, stretched out immediately, and the faith that is commended elsewhere in the Gospels is repeatedly the size of a grain of mustard seed. Faith in Scripture is not a force a man generates and aims; it is a receiving, and its object does the work. Treating it as leverage turns the gospel into a technique and lays on sufferers a burden the apostles never laid.

The opposite error reads the rebuke as a verdict of unbelief and so teaches the weak to doubt whether they believe at all. Christ's own term forbids it: little faith is faith. The 1689 Confession allows that faith is different in degrees, weak or strong, may be often and many ways assailed and weakened, but gets the victory, growing up in many to the attainment of a full assurance. The principle to recover is pastoral and plain. A sinking disciple is to cry out as Peter did, and the hand that caught him is the same hand still, strong enough for small faith that calls on the right name.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek oligopistos, of little faith — oligos, little; pistis, faith; with distazō, to waver between two minds, the verb of the question that follows.

expand to see more

Greek oligos, little, small, or few in number or degree.

Greek pistis, faith, trust, or firm persuasion resting on another.

Greek oligopistos, of little faith, used only by Christ in the New Testament.

Greek distazō, to waver or stand in two minds, hence to doubt.

Spoken after the hand was already stretched out and holding, Matthew 14:31.

Usage

"O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?"
